quote: Giebt es im Raume noch andere umkehrbar eindeutige Transformationen, die nicht linear sind oder durch lineare sich zusammensetzen lassen?
english: Are there in space other one-to-one transformations that are not linear or cannot be composed from linear ones?
topic: Notes on reducing birational (Cremona) transformations of the plane to quadratic or linear ones, a question about such transformations in space with a reference to Nöther in Math. Ann. Bd. 3, and the start of a proof that a series of continuous functions converging continuously on an interval converges uniformly.

triage.modern_statement: In modern terms, Hilbert is asking about the Cremona group Cr_3 = Bir(P^3), the group of birational self-maps of projective 3-space. In the plane, the Noether–Castelnuovo theorem says every Cremona transformation is a composition of projective linear maps and the standard quadratic involution. The question is whether something similar holds in space: is every birational map of P^3 a composition of projective linear (PGL_4) maps, perhaps together with a few simple extra maps such as the standard involution? Read word for word, the question 'are there nonlinear birational maps of space' is trivial, because the standard cubic involution (x_i -> 1/x_i) is one. The real research content is the generation question.
triage.answered_by: The answer is no: there is no Noether–Castelnuovo-type theorem in dimension 3 or higher. Hilda P. Hudson (1927) showed that the Cremona group in dimension n>=3 cannot be generated by elements of bounded degree. Ivan Pan later sharpened this (Hudson–Pan theorem): Cr_n is never generated by PGL_{n+1} together with any set of maps of bounded degree, or by countably many elements when the field is uncountable. Blanc–Hedén (2014/15) showed that in odd dimension there are simple maps outside the group generated by PGL and the standard involution. Blanc–Lamy–Zimmermann (Acta Math. 226, 2021) showed that Cr_n for n>=3 is not generated even by linear and Jonquières elements.

evidence.claim: In the plane, the Cremona group is generated by the standard quadratic transformation and PGL(3) (Noether–Castelnuovo). Hudson (1927) showed that in dimension at least 3 it is not generated by its elements of degree bounded by any fixed integer, so there is no simple analogue.

Hudson–Pan theorem: for n>=3, one needs as many algebraic families of generators as there are families of smooth hypersurfaces of P^{n-1} of degree >= n+2, so the Cremona group cannot be generated by maps of bounded degree.

Hudson and Pan showed that Cr_n(k) is never generated by PGL_{n+1}(k) together with any set of maps of bounded degree, or by countably many elements when k is uncountable. No explicit generating set is currently known for n>=3.

Blanc–Hedén studied the group generated by PGL(n+1) and the standard involution of degree n. In odd dimension they found simple elements that only contract rational hypersurfaces but do not belong to that group.
Blanc–Lamy–Zimmermann, 'Quotients of higher-dimensional Cremona groups' (Acta Math. 226(2), 2021): the Cremona group of rank n>=3 is not generated by linear and Jonquières elements.

triage.why: Hilbert's wording is short. Given the context on the page (plane Cremona transformations reduced to quadratic and linear ones, plus a reference to Noether in Math. Ann. 3), it most plausibly asks whether a Noether-type generation theorem holds in space. Read literally it is trivial, since nonlinear birational maps of space exist. As a generation question it was answered in the negative: Hudson (1927), then Pan, Blanc–Hedén, and Blanc–Lamy–Zimmermann (2021). It is not among Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. The related question of finding an explicit generating set for Cr_n (n>=3) remains open, and Cremona groups in higher dimension are an active research area.
